quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, Ireland per the tree) headed a Schuylkill County household in 1850 that held Patrick, age 5, recorded as born in Ireland. The 1870 census, a name-searchable national collection, tests whether Thomas and Patrick (about 25) still share a household or Patrick heads his own, and whether a Thomas of the right age is still present. The objective says Patrick was born in Pennsylvania, but the 1850 entry and the tree's birth fact both say Ireland, so this search assumes neither. No 1870 search is logged.

Requested by the researcher: the 1870 United States Federal Census on Ancestry, a name-searchable index. It is a paid derivative transcription, so it cross-checks the FamilySearch image from the item before it rather than proving anything alone. Search Thomas and Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County and compare dwelling, ages and birthplaces with the FamilySearch result. A mismatch means the image needs checking.

The tree cites the 1860 census for the parent-child link, but no 1860 search is logged. Patrick would be about 15, so the 1860 household should show whether he is still listed with Thomas and whether a wife and other children are present, which supplies sibling candidates. The collection is name-searchable.

The tree cites a Pennsylvania death certificate for Patrick's death on 1908-03-12 for the parent-child link, but no log entry shows the certificate was examined. A 1908 state certificate, which is the first year of statewide death registration, normally names the father and mother and their birthplaces. Read the certificate for the parent names and the informant. Whatever it says is a claim by the informant, not proof of parentage.

A dedicated item for the parents' marriage, separate from any child record. Thomas Flynn's marriage record, if found in the county marriage collections (name-searchable), confirms the couple as a unit and gives the mother's maiden name, which the census omits. It dates their union against Patrick's birth around 1845, which corroborates Thomas as father but does not by itself establish that Patrick is their child. Thomas may have married more than once, so the wife's surname on this record is not settled until the other marriages are checked.

The baptism of Patrick, the only record that places the child with the parents at birth. The register start date is not in the locality entry, and the birth may have been in Ireland, which the 1850 census states. The baptism may therefore sit in a Pennsylvania parish register held by the diocese, or may not exist in Pennsylvania at all. Search the name-searchable Pennsylvania births and christenings collection, and treat an Irish baptism as the target if no Pennsylvania entry turns up. The Catholic parishes of the anthracite region stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia, so the Diocese of Scranton is not the place to look.

A FAN item for the parentage question. The 1850 household holds other children besides Patrick, if any are listed. Marriage and baptism records for those siblings, in the county marriage and birth collections, often name Thomas and the mother as parents. Each one tests the same couple from another angle and can give the maiden name when the marriage record does not. The item is needed because the parentage question requires at least one associate-directed search.

Thomas Flynn's will or administration, filed with the Schuylkill County Register of Wills from 1811, is a primary parentage source if it names Patrick as a son or heir. The window follows Thomas's own lifespan (born about 1818), not the subject's, since he is the creator of the file, and his death year is not yet known. The probate collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the county dockets, not a name search.

The 1850 to 1880 mortality schedules are a name-searchable national collection. A Thomas Flynn who died in the census year before 1880 would be listed with his age, birthplace and cause of death, which fixes his death year for the probate window and can name a place of death. This does not establish parentage, but it narrows when the probate and burial records should be searched.

Pennsylvania cemetery records, a name-searchable collection, for Thomas Flynn's burial and for Patrick's burial in 1908. Burial entries sometimes name a parent or a family plot that places Patrick with Thomas. Treat each as a lead to check against the census and probate records, not as proof.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown: Patrick Flynn appears in the 1850 census in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household. Co-enumeration is indirect evidence that supports but does not prove parentage. Post-1860 censuses, probate, and church records have not yet been searched.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn's 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate. The tree already cites it (source S3) on the death fact, but no assertion from it is in research.json, so its parent names, birthplace and informant are unread. Statewide death certificates begin in 1906, making this the earliest civil record that can name a father. The informant is likely a household member and should be weighed as such. Collection is name-searchable.

The 1880 federal census is the first to record each person's relationship to head and the birthplace of each person's parents. It tests whether Patrick (about 35) is still in Thomas Flynn's household, whether Thomas is recorded as his father, and what birthplace is given for Patrick's parents. Collection is name-searchable.

Baptism of Patrick, about 1845. The tree gives his birthplace as Ireland (from the 1850 census age and birthplace), while the objective says Pennsylvania; a Pennsylvania baptism would settle which is right. Pennsylvania civil birth registration began only in 1906, so a baptism is the earliest record that could name both parents. Schuylkill's Roman Catholic registers are held by parishes or the Diocese of Philadelphia, so the church and christening collections, which are name-searchable, are the route. If no Pennsylvania baptism exists, Irish origin needs a locality survey before any Irish item is planned.

Marriage of Thomas Flynn (born about 1818) to Patrick's mother, dated before Patrick's birth. This marriage supplies the mother's name, and by its date it corroborates Thomas as father; it does not by itself show Patrick is their child. The mother's name is unknown, so search on Thomas's surname with the county and a bride with an Irish surname. Marriage collections in Pennsylvania (compiled 1700-1900, statewide to 1940, and church marriages) are name-searchable. The marriage may have taken place in Ireland; check that only if no Pennsylvania entry appears.

The tree's ParentChild relationship cites the 1860 federal census (source S2), but research.json has no log entry or assertion from it. This item reads the 1860 household to confirm whether Patrick is listed with Thomas Flynn and to get the mother's given name and age, which can identify her. Collection is name-searchable.

The 1870 federal census tests whether the mother is still in the household after the 1860 count, and whether Patrick, about 25, remains with Thomas. Any death or absence of a woman of the right age can be read against the 1835-1846 marriage. Collection is name-searchable.

Companion to the parents' marriage item: a later marriage of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County. If Thomas remarried, the bride's name in that record must be tested against the mother's identity, so the 1835-1846 marriage's bride is not treated as his first wife without proof. Marriage collections are name-searchable.

Will or administration of Thomas Flynn, or of the mother if she died first, held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills (probate available from 1811). A will or intestate estate could name Patrick as a son. Thomas was born about 1818, so his death could fall anywhere from about 1845 to 1900, which sets the window. The probate collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the county's dockets, not a name search.

Burial of Thomas Flynn, or of the mother, in a Schuylkill cemetery. Burial entries often give age, birthplace and the name of a spouse or next of kin, which can supply the mother's name or a birthplace. Cemetery collections for Pennsylvania are name-searchable.

Associates test for the parentage question. The 1850 census was searched only for Patrick, and the neighbouring households around dwelling 84 were not read. Irish-born Flynn or related households next door may be kin or may name the family. Also read the godparents and witnesses on any Schuylkill baptisms of Patrick's siblings that name Thomas Flynn as father. Both the census and church collections are name-searchable.

Patrick's own marriage in Schuylkill County. His baptism may not exist in the Pennsylvania registers, so the marriage entry is a route to his birthplace and parents. Marriage entries sometimes give birthplace or the father's name. County marriage collections are name-searchable.

## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845-1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). Indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate names Thomas Flynn as his father. Direct evidence, secondary informant (son-in-law James Brown).

### Conflict Resolution

Birthplace conflict resolved: Ireland (censuses) over Pennsylvania (death cert) per informant proximity and source independence.

### Assessment

Rated **Probable** pending exhaustive declaration.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

items.question: Besides Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph, who were the other children of Thomas Hale (b. about 1810, Pennsylvania; d. 1868, Greene County, Ohio) and his wife Sarah?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. The tree holds the couple and five children; no records have been searched yet for any others.

entry.rationale: The 1850 household of Thomas and Sarah Hale should list every child under about 14 living with them, so any child besides Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph who was at home in 1850 should appear by name and age. The United States Census, 1850 is name-searchable (loc_001 nationalCollections). Search both parents' names and check neighbouring households for a child living apart.

The 1860 household should show children aged about 13 to 24, including older children who had left the 1850 household and any child born after 1850. The United States Census, 1860 is name-searchable (loc_001 nationalCollections). Children who had left home may appear as a separate household or as hired labour, so record those names too.

The 1840 household may show a child born before Mary (about 1836) or a child born 1836-1840 while still an infant. Mary is the earliest child in the tree, so a pre-1836 child would be missing from it. The United States, Census, 1840 is name-searchable (loc_001 nationalCollections). Ages in 1840 are coarse, so match on household composition.

Thomas died in 1868, so the 1870 census should show Sarah as head or as a member of a child's household, with any younger children still at home. The United States Census, 1870 is name-searchable (loc_001 nationalCollections). Check each Hale household in the county for a child who has married and moved out.

Sarah, as a widow in 1880, may still live with an unmarried child or a child's family. The United States, Census, 1880 is name-searchable (loc_001 nationalCollections). A child who is not in the household may still be named in the relationship column, so check for a relation to Sarah.

A birth or christening record for each child names both parents, so searching Thomas Hale and Sarah as parents may surface children not yet in the tree. Ohio, Births and Christenings, 1821-1962 is name-searchable (loc_001 collections). Search by the parents' names with no given name, because the unknown child's name is what is sought.

The civil birth registration in Ohio began in 1867 at state level, so births from 1836 to 1850 in Greene County are likely recorded only in church registers. Ohio, Church Records, 1762-2008 is name-searchable (loc_001 collections). Use it as a fallback for the births item if that item returns no 1834-1850 entries for the couple.

The marriage of Thomas Hale and Sarah should bracket the births of the children, as Mary was born about 1836. Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2016 is name-searchable (loc_001 collections). The marriage record gives Sarah's maiden name, which is needed to search for her family and any earlier marriage. Check for a second marriage of Sarah, because a half-sibling from an earlier marriage would not be a child of Thomas.

Thomas died in 1868 in Greene County, and Sarah's death is undated, so their death or burial entries may name surviving children or give Sarah's age and birthplace. Ohio, Deaths and Burials, 1854-1997 is name-searchable (loc_001 collections). Use Ohio, County Death Records, 1840-2001 for the same search if the first returns nothing.

Thomas's estate file, opened after his death in 1868, may name each heir, including every surviving child. Probate was held by the Court of Common Pleas until 1852 and by the Greene County Probate Court after, so the file should be in the Probate Court. Ohio, Probate Records, 1789-1996 is browse-only (loc_001 collections), so this is an image browse of the estate docket. The window runs to 1895 because Sarah's estate may be filed decades later.

The sons John, William and Joseph were aged about 14 to 27 during the Civil War, and any unknown son of that age would also be eligible. Service papers often name the parents and home county. Ohio, Military Discharge Records, 1834-2004 is name-searchable (loc_001 collections). Search by the surname Hale with Greene County as the home county, and read each record for named parents or siblings.

A neighbour-level check. Tax lists name the Hale household and any adult child who owned property or lived apart, so they may show a child not yet found in the census. Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1887 is name-searchable (loc_001 collections), but confirm the county is covered before reading results as complete.

Plan pl_001 is ready with twelve items for finding the other children of Thomas and Sarah Hale. items.rationale: The 1850 household of Thomas and Sarah Hale should list every child under about 14 living with them, so any child besides Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph who was at home in 1850 should appear by name and age. The United States Census, 1850 is name-searchable (loc_001 nationalCollections). Search both parents' names and check neighbouring households for a child living apart.

The 1860 household should show children aged about 13 to 24, including older children who had left the 1850 household and any child born after 1850. The United States Census, 1860 is name-searchable (loc_001 nationalCollections). Children who had left home may appear as a separate household or as hired labour, so record those names too.

The 1840 household may show a child born before Mary (about 1836) or a child born 1836-1840 while still an infant. Mary is the earliest child in the tree, so a pre-1836 child would be missing from it. The United States, Census, 1840 is name-searchable (loc_001 nationalCollections). Ages in 1840 are coarse, so match on household composition.

Thomas died in 1868, so the 1870 census should show Sarah as head or as a member of a child's household, with any younger children still at home. The United States Census, 1870 is name-searchable (loc_001 nationalCollections). Check each Hale household in the county for a child who has married and moved out.

Sarah, as a widow in 1880, may still live with an unmarried child or a child's family. The United States, Census, 1880 is name-searchable (loc_001 nationalCollections). A child who is not in the household may still be named in the relationship column, so check for a relation to Sarah.

A birth or christening record for each child names both parents, so searching Thomas Hale and Sarah as parents may surface children not yet in the tree. Ohio, Births and Christenings, 1821-1962 is name-searchable (loc_001 collections). Search by the parents' names with no given name, because the unknown child's name is what is sought.

The civil birth registration in Ohio began in 1867 at state level, so births from 1836 to 1850 in Greene County are likely recorded only in church registers. Ohio, Church Records, 1762-2008 is name-searchable (loc_001 collections). Use it as a fallback for the births item if that item returns no 1834-1850 entries for the couple.

The marriage of Thomas Hale and Sarah should bracket the births of the children, as Mary was born about 1836. Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2016 is name-searchable (loc_001 collections). The marriage record gives Sarah's maiden name, which is needed to search for her family and any earlier marriage. Check for a second marriage of Sarah, because a half-sibling from an earlier marriage would not be a child of Thomas.

Thomas died in 1868 in Greene County, and Sarah's death is undated, so their death or burial entries may name surviving children or give Sarah's age and birthplace. Ohio, Deaths and Burials, 1854-1997 is name-searchable (loc_001 collections). Use Ohio, County Death Records, 1840-2001 for the same search if the first returns nothing.

Thomas's estate file, opened after his death in 1868, may name each heir, including every surviving child. Probate was held by the Court of Common Pleas until 1852 and by the Greene County Probate Court after, so the file should be in the Probate Court. Ohio, Probate Records, 1789-1996 is browse-only (loc_001 collections), so this is an image browse of the estate docket. The window runs to 1895 because Sarah's estate may be filed decades later.

The sons John, William and Joseph were aged about 14 to 27 during the Civil War, and any unknown son of that age would also be eligible. Service papers often name the parents and home county. Ohio, Military Discharge Records, 1834-2004 is name-searchable (loc_001 collections). Search by the surname Hale with Greene County as the home county, and read each record for named parents or siblings.

A neighbour-level check. Tax lists name the Hale household and any adult child who owned property or lived apart, so they may show a child not yet found in the census. Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1887 is name-searchable (loc_001 collections), but confirm the county is covered before reading results as complete.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

The marriage gives the mother's maiden name only if it was her first; a marriage in Ireland before emigration would not appear here. It corroborates the father by date relative to Patrick's birth but does not by itself place Patrick with the couple.

Burial of Thomas Flynn, in the Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 and Pennsylvania Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950 collections (both name-searchable). quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: The tree makes Thomas Flynn (I2, b. about 1818, Ireland) the parent of Patrick (I1) on the strength of the 1850 and 1860 censuses and the 1908 death certificate, but neither census states relationships. The 1880 census is the first to give each member's relationship to the head, so it is the direct test of whether Patrick is recorded as Thomas's son. The 1880 national census is name-searchable. This item does not settle the birthplace conflict (Ireland on the censuses, Pennsylvania on the death certificate).

The 1870 census is the enumeration between the 1860 census and the 1880 census that can still show the Thomas Flynn household. It may name Thomas's wife, which no census so far has done, and it shows whether Patrick is still at home and whether Thomas is still alive in Schuylkill County. The 1870 national census is name-searchable.

Patrick died in 1908, so the 1900 census can place him in his own household with a stated relationship and his age. If his mother was widowed or living with him, the 1900 entry may name her and give the number of children she bore, which bears on the parentage question. The 1900 national census is name-searchable.

A will or administration of Thomas Flynn naming Patrick as a son would be direct parentage evidence, and it would also name the wife. Schuylkill County was formed in 1811, so its Register of Wills holds the file. The window is sized to Thomas's lifespan (born about 1818), not the subject's, so it runs from 1850 to about 1900. The state probate collection for Pennsylvania is browse-only, so this item is an image browse of the county's dockets, not a name search.

Fallback for the probate browse. Run volume_search on the Schuylkill County probate image groups to find which volumes cover 1850-1900 and whether any are full-text searchable. This item carries the same question as the primary probate item: whether Thomas named Patrick as a son.

A dedicated item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn to Patrick's mother. The marriage record supplies her maiden name if this was her first marriage, confirms the couple as a unit, and by its date relative to Patrick's birth around 1845 corroborates Thomas as father. It does not by itself prove that Patrick is their child. The County Marriages and Civil Marriages collections are name-searchable. The marriage may have taken place in Ireland, so a negative result here does not rule out an Irish marriage.

Companion item to the parents' marriage. Thomas or his wife may have married again after Patrick's birth, so the surname the marriage record gives her may not be her birth surname. Search all marriage records naming Thomas Flynn as groom in the county in this period to test whether the wife's marriage was her first. Name-searchable collections apply.

Burial entries for Thomas Flynn and his wife give death dates and sometimes ages or birthplaces. They bound the period in which Patrick could have been a child in the household and may show a family plot with other children's names. The Pennsylvania cemetery records collection is name-searchable.

Patrick's own marriage and his daughter's marriage to James Brown, the death certificate informant. Marriage entries sometimes name the parents of each party, which would test the death certificate's naming of Thomas. James Brown's household in the 1900 census is also an associate source. This is the FAN item for the parentage question. The County Marriages collection is name-searchable.

The birthplace conflict (Ireland on the censuses, Pennsylvania on the death certificate) can be tested by searching for a Pennsylvania baptism of Patrick, son of Thomas Flynn, in the years around 1845. The Pennsylvania Births and Christenings collection is name-searchable. A baptism here would support a Pennsylvania birth and a father named in the register. The Roman Catholic registers for Schuylkill stayed at the parish or diocese, not the county, so a negative county result does not rule out a parish record.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.question: Who were the other children born to Bridget Halloran and her first husband, John Doyle, beyond the one already identified (Ellen Doyle)?
items.rationale: An 1900 census entry (log_002) records Bridget as mother of 9 children with only 2 living, but only one child (Ellen Doyle) has been identified so far, found incidentally rather than through a direct search for Doyle offspring. This is a pedigree gap directly within the project objective. No plan has yet been written for this question.

items.notes: Pennsylvania County Marriages: Martin Kearney m. Bridget (Doyle) Halloran, 1879, Schuylkill County. Confirms Bridget's second marriage and that her first married surname was Doyle, maiden name Halloran. Found incidentally while researching an unrelated question; not part of any plan.

query.description: 1900 census page image, Schuylkill County, PA - Kearney household, fertility columns

items.notes: Original 1900 census image for the Kearney household: 'Mother of how many children' = 9; 'Number of these children living' = 2. Indicates Bridget bore ~9 children, most likely during the earlier Doyle marriage, with only 2 surviving to 1900. Only one of the two, Ellen Doyle, has been identified by name so far. Roughly 7-8 children remain unidentified/undocumented.

Pennsylvania County Marriages: entry for Ellen Doyle's own marriage, with her parents recorded as John Doyle and Bridget Halloran. Independently identifies the first husband's given name as JOHN Doyle. Found incidentally; not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Bridget Halloran's first marriage was to John Doyle (log_001 and log_003). The 1870 federal census is the most likely listing of John, Bridget and their children in one household, with ages and birthplaces that place each child. The 1870 United States census is name-searchable. Schuylkill County has been a separate county since 1811, so no boundary split affects this search.

The 1860 federal census may show the earliest Doyle household, before the 1870 count. The 1860 United States census is name-searchable. Bridget was born about 1838, so an 1860 household could list only the first children. Test every child at home for a Doyle surname.

Martin Kearney married Bridget in 1879 (log_001). The 1880 census household of Martin and Bridget Kearney may list her Doyle children as stepchildren, and shows which children were still at home after John Doyle's death. The 1880 United States census is name-searchable.

The 1900 census image for the Kearney household (log_002) records Bridget as mother of 9 children with 2 living. The household members named on that page have not been transcribed into the plan. Re-read the full household and the neighboring households for Doyle-surname children. The 1900 United States census is name-searchable.

The 1900 count of 9 children with 2 living means about 7 died young. The mortality schedules for the years before the 1860, 1870 and 1880 counts list deaths in the household during the census year and name each deceased child. The United States Mortality Schedules 1850-1880 are name-searchable.

Birth registration statewide began only in 1906 (locality quirk), so baptisms are the main birth record for children born 1856-1882. The Pennsylvania Births and Christenings 1709-1950 collection is name-searchable. Search for children whose father is John Doyle and whose mother is Bridget Halloran; Catholic baptisms usually record the mother's maiden name, so the Halloran name is the key term.

Fallback for the baptism search. Roman Catholic sacramental registers for Schuylkill County stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia and are held at the parish, not the county. If the indexed baptism search returns nothing, browse the church register images for the Doyle family's parish image by image. Some church films for the anthracite region are browse-only.

Delayed birth records cover children whose births were never registered in their own time. The Pennsylvania Delayed Birth Records 1780-1977 collection is name-searchable, and a delayed record for a Doyle child would name both parents.

Children who died young are often buried in the Doyle or Halloran family plot. The Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials 1720-1999 and Pennsylvania Cemetery Records ca. 1700-ca. 1950 collections are name-searchable. Search for Doyle children and for Bridget under both Doyle and Kearney.

Marriage records of the surviving children often name their mother. The Pennsylvania County Marriages 1775-1991 and Pennsylvania Marriages 1709-1940 collections are name-searchable. Search for brides and grooms whose mother is Bridget Halloran, Bridget Doyle or Bridget Kearney.

John Doyle's estate or guardianship file, held by the county Register of Wills, would list his heirs and minor children. The window is sized to John Doyle's plausible lifespan, from the first child's birth to about 60 years later. The Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Schuylkill dockets.

Bridget's own estate, if she died after the 1900 census, would name her surviving children. Her lifespan sets the window, from the 1900 count to about 30 years later. The Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse.

Obituaries of the surviving children, or of Bridget, name surviving siblings and parents. The Schuylkill Haven Funeral Home Obituary Cards 1914-2007 and Pennsylvania Obituaries 1977-2010 collections are name-searchable. Search for the Doyle surname together with Halloran or Kearney.

- Bridget Halloran (I1) is the subject. Her tree record has a birth about 1838 in Ireland and a couple link to John Doyle (I2).
- Ellen Doyle (I3) is the one identified child, a daughter of Bridget and John.
- log_001: 1879 Schuylkill marriage of Martin Kearney to Bridget (Doyle) Halloran.
- log_002: 1900 census image for the Kearney household, Bridget recorded as mother of 9 children with 2 living.
- log_003: Ellen Doyle's marriage record, naming her parents as John Doyle and Bridget Halloran.

Plan items for pl_001, in execution order:
1. pli_001, 1870 census, Schuylkill County (FamilySearch, name-searchable): the likely household of John, Bridget and the children.
2. pli_002, 1860 census, Schuylkill County (name-searchable): the earliest Doyle household.
3. pli_003, 1880 census, Schuylkill County (name-searchable): the Kearney household, for Doyle children as stepchildren.
4. pli_004, 1900 census, Schuylkill County (name-searchable): re-read the full Kearney household and neighbors from the existing image.
5. pli_005, mortality schedules 1859-1880 (name-searchable): the 7 children who likely died young.
6. pli_006, baptisms 1856-1882 (Pennsylvania Births and Christenings, name-searchable): searched by father John Doyle and mother Halloran.
7. pli_007, fallback for pli_006, browse of Catholic parish register images (browse-only): used if the indexed baptism search returns nothing.
8. pli_008, delayed birth records 1856-1900 (name-searchable).
9. pli_009, deaths, burials and cemetery records 1858-1950 (name-searchable).
10. pli_010, marriages of the children 1875-1920 (county and state marriage collections, name-searchable), searched by mother's name.
11. pli_011, John Doyle's estate or guardianship file 1858-1918 (Register of Wills; browse-only).
12. pli_012, Bridget's estate 1900-1930 (browse-only).
13. pli_013, obituary cards and obituaries 1914-2010 (name-searchable).

Gaps in the plan: no item covers Ellen Doyle's marriage witnesses or sureties, which are the usual route to siblings, so that is the first thing to add. The plan has 13 items, one above the usual size, and I kept them all because you asked for exhaustive coverage.

Hand-back: search-records — run pli_001 through pli_013 in sequence (pli_007 only if pli_006 finds nothing). None of the items needs search-external-sites.

items.guide_markdown:
## Stagstrup Sogn, Thisted Amt, Denmark - late 1700s

For a male subject born 1779, two record classes carry parentage. Church books (kirkeboeger) hold the baptism naming both parents. The military levy rolls (laegdsruller), kept from 1789, enroll every boy under his father's name from childhood - direct evidence of the father. Danish patronymics (Nielsen = son of Niels) point to the father's given name but not the specific man. The Stagstrup register is only ~3% indexed, so plan to browse images.

entry.rationale: The subject was born 20 Aug 1779 in Stagstrup parish. His baptism entry in the Stagstrup church book should name both parents, the most direct route to the father's given name. loc_001 says the Stagstrup register is only about 3% name-indexed, so this is a browse of the register images for mid to late 1779, not a name search.

Per the Denmark military records page, boys were enrolled in the levy rolls (laegdsruller) from birth, and loc_001 notes each son is entered directly beneath his father's name. A 1789-1792 Stagstrup roll should list the subject as a boy under his father, which is direct parentage evidence. The FamilySearch collection Denmark, Military Conscription Rolls, 1789-1792 is name-searchable. Follow the parish and supplemental numbers if he moved.

A dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other, in the Stagstrup church book before August 1779. It confirms the couple as a unit and may give the mother's maiden name, but only if this was her first marriage. Search each marriage record of the mother, since a remarriage would change which surname is hers. The marriage corroborates a father named only indirectly; it does not by itself establish that the subject is their child.

The Denmark Census 1787-1930 collection is name-searchable. The 1787 household listing for Stagstrup should show a head named Niels with a boy of about seven or eight, which is a household link between the father and the subject. Read the relationship-to-head column in the schedule.

The 1801 census for Stagstrup is name-searchable within the Denmark Census 1787-1930 collection. At age about 21 the subject may be listed as a son in his father's household, which would place him with the father, and the father's status (living or dead, and any widow) bears on the death question.

FAN item. Browse the Stagstrup baptism register for siblings of the subject, and for godparents, in the years around 1779. A sibling's baptism naming the same parents is a second independent link to the father, and a godparent may be a relative who names him. loc_001 says the register is only about 3% name-indexed, so browse images.

Denmark Probate Indexes 1674-1851 is name-searchable. The window runs to 1851 because a father of a child born in 1779 could die anywhere from 1779 into the 1830s or later, so the window is sized to his lifespan, not the subject's. A probate naming Mikkel as a son would be direct evidence and would give the father's death date.

Once the father's given name and farm are known from items 1 to 6, search the Stagstrup burial register for his burial. The entry states the age and gives the death date, which answers the second half of the objective. It depends on an identified father, so it is sequenced last.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Per the locality quirk, also search under the second given name 'Margaretha' alone. The place service did not resolve Württemberg to a standard place, so the parish must be identified from the register itself.

Marriage of the candidate parents, not the subject's own marriage. It supplies the mother's maiden name and dates the father's union relative to the 1792 birth. It does not by itself prove the child is theirs, so it must be paired with the baptism (pli_001). If the mother married more than once, a surname that differs between records would need a marriage record for each of her marriages. Search the name-searchable collection 'Germany Marriages, 1558-1929' (loc_001).

The subject's own marriage, planned because the register may not reach back to her baptism. Marriage entries often state the bride's parents and home parish, which would name the parents or the origin parish. Search 'Germany Marriages, 1558-1929' (loc_001), under 'Anna Margaretha' and 'Margaretha'.

The subject's own death or burial entry, dated after her last known life event. Death and burial entries often state age, parents or birthplace, the usual route to an origin when the baptism is out of reach. The FamilySearch collections named in loc_001 are birth, baptism and marriage registers only, so this entry must be reached through the parish register images or the state archives, not a name search of those collections.

FAN item. Baptisms of siblings and of godparents recorded in the same parish register name the same parents, and the sponsors often belong to the family's kin. Search the baptism register for the parents' other children and for sponsors who share the surname, to test the parentage. This is required for a parentage question.

Estate inventory or division of a father who died after 1792. Its window is sized to the father's likely lifespan, not the subject's: a father of a child born in 1792 could die anywhere from the early 1790s to about 1840. Fallback for the parents' marriage item (pli_002) on a paid repository, if the free indexed search does not return the couple. Searched on the surname and the candidate parents' given names only; it is a discovery step and the result is verified against the original register image.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Dedicated item for Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother, required for parentage. I superseded pl_002 and wrote the new active plan pl_003. Nothing else was changed, and I did not touch the completed items.

Facts from the survey that bear on the question:
- The 1850 census (log_001) places Patrick, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household in Schuylkill County.
- The 1860 census (log_004, pli_004) places Patrick, age 15, in Thomas Flynn's household, so Thomas was alive in mid-1860. This fits a c.1865 death.
- The Pennsylvania death certificate for Patrick (log_005, pli_005) names Thomas Flynn as father, with son-in-law James Brown as informant.
- The tree records Thomas Flynn as born c.1818 in Ireland, and Patrick as born c.1845 in Ireland. The objective says Pennsylvania, so the birthplace conflict is open.

Plan items in pl_003, in order:
1. pli_007, probate, Schuylkill County, 1860-1870, FamilySearch. Browse-only image search of the Register of Wills files. Estate papers could name Patrick as a son and list appraisers, bondsmen and creditors as FAN leads.
2. pli_008, death or burial entry, Schuylkill County, 1860-1870, FamilySearch. Name-searchable. Fixes the year and place of Thomas's death before the probate search.
3. pli_009, cemetery record, Schuylkill County, 1860-1870, FamilySearch. Fallback for pli_008.
4. pli_010, 1870 census, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. Name-searchable. Shows whether the widow's household includes Patrick.
5. pli_011, marriage search for Thomas's widow remarrying, Schuylkill County, 1865-1870, FamilySearch. Name-searchable. A remarriage record could name her as widow of Thomas.
6. pli_012, the parents' marriage, Schuylkill County, 1835-1846, FamilySearch. Name-searchable. This is the dedicated parentage item the method requires. It falls outside your 1860-1870 window because it must predate Patrick's birth, and it may be in Ireland rather than Pennsylvania.
7. pli_013, Pennsylvania Civil War volunteer register, 1861-1865, FamilySearch. Name-searchable. Checks whether Patrick enlisted.

The plan has no FamilySearch hints item because the tree export shows no record identifier for Patrick.

Two notes. The 1908 death item (pli_005) is already completed and concerns Patrick's own death, so its window is unchanged. I have not searched any of the new items yet.

---

A Civil War volunteer register check closes the plan.
